Based on the search results, here's what I found about Teresa Torres and the product trio concept:

## The Product Trio

A product trio is typically comprised of a product manager, a designer, and a software engineer. Teresa Torres, the product discovery coach who popularized the framework in her 2021 book Continuous Discovery Habits, defines it this way: "A product trio is a cross-functional team that includes a product manager, a designer, and a software engineer who are working together to discover products."

## Continuous Discovery

Continuous discovery habits are five practices defined by Teresa Torres in her book Continuous Discovery Habits: (1) interview at least one customer per week, (2) map opportunities in an opportunity solution tree, (3) surface and test assumptions before building, (4) run small experiments continuously, and (5) involve the whole product trio (PM, designer, engineer) in discovery.

## Collaborative Working Model

Popularized by Teresa Torres in Continuous Discovery Habits, the trio replaces serial handoffs ("PM defines, designer mocks up, engineer builds") with shared customer learning. Product trios need to conduct research together so they can work from the same knowledge base. Second, they need to externalize their thinking visually to stay aligned.

The key innovation of the product trio model is that all three roles participate in discovery activities together, rather than working in silos and handing off work sequentially.

Based on the search results, I found detailed information about Marty Cagan's framework of the four big risks in product discovery and the role of engineers in addressing feasibility risk.

## Marty Cagan's Four Big Risks in Product Discovery

The four big risks are: Value risk (whether customers will buy it or users will choose to use it), Usability risk (whether users can figure out how to use it), Feasibility risk (whether our engineers can build what we need with the time, skills and technology we have), and Business viability risk (whether this solution also works for the various aspects of our business).

## Engineers and Feasibility Risk

The Product Lead Engineer is responsible for the feasibility risk, and overall accountable for the product's delivery. Engineering should be involved early in the discovery process to address this risk before committing resources to development.

## Purpose of Addressing These Risks

These risks should be attacked during discovery, cheaply, with prototypes — before anyone writes production code. Shipping-stage failures almost always trace to a specific risk the team either skipped or deferred.

## RACI Matrix Overview

RACI is an acronym for responsible, accountable, consulted, informed. A RACI matrix is a decision-making framework that assigns four roles to every task or decision: Responsible (executes), Accountable (owns outcome), Consulted (provides input), and Informed (receives updates).

## Application to Product Roles

RACI matrix lays out the responsibility chart for different tasks or deliverables, with the idea being to layout the role the product manager and product owner will take against each of these activities. In the context of product ownership, the RACI matrix serves as a blueprint for defining the roles of product managers, developers, designers, stakeholders, and other team members, ensuring that everyone understands their contributions to the product lifecycle, from ideation to launch.

## Decision Rights and Architecture

Decision rights architecture defines authority boundaries, and the RACI framework translates those rights into daily accountability for specific tasks. Only one person can be accountable for each decision, preventing overlapping responsibilities.

## Benefits

Organizations using RACI frameworks report 70% fewer "who decides" questions and 25% faster cycle times. It clearly separates who is Responsible for completing the task and who is Accountable for its outcome, eliminating confusion, and defines who needs to be Consulted and Informed, ensuring the right people are involved at the right time.

## Key Concepts

The "build trap" is one of the biggest pitfalls in product development, resulting in a bloated product, poor product-market fit, and a disconnect between business goals and user needs.

One of the core problems is when stakeholders dictate what gets built rather than using user insights, or when product managers focus on backlog management instead of problem-solving.

## Architecture and Dictating Solutions

In feature factory environments, product managers act as order takers, designers produce specifications without user validation, and engineers are judged on their ability to clear tickets from a backlog. This represents the problematic pattern where decisions are handed down without proper architectural consideration or stakeholder input.

## Ignored Backlogs and Failure Modes

Most product backlogs are graveyards of stale ideas—hundreds of tickets filed over months or years, most of them irrelevant by the time anyone looks at them. Feature factories rarely scrap work or acknowledge failure because the goal is output, not learning.

## Root Causes

The root cause is almost always the same: the organization measures output, not outcomes. Across engagements, 40-60% of engineering time in these teams goes to features that will never connect to a revenue outcome.

"Stakeholders dictate what gets built, not user insights — If your priorities are set by executives instead of data-driven learning, you're likely stuck in a feature factory"

"Success is measured in story points completed, not outcomes achieved — Agile isn't about moving faster; it's about moving smarter"

"A PM's job isn't to manage tickets; it's to deeply understand users and drive value" — when this responsibility shifts to stakeholders, the trap tightens.

"It assumes you know what users need months in advance, which is rarely accurate" when executives pre-determine roadmaps without validation.

## Technical Consequences
"Every feature adds technical debt, expands the bug surface area, and requires ongoing support. This increases operational costs and slows down future development"

"Each additional button, setting, or workflow creates unnecessary friction, making the product less intuitive" as maintenance burdens accumulate.

## Remedies & Decision Authority
"Use data, user research, and A/B testing to guide decisions, not just stakeholder opinions" — shifting authority to evidence-based approaches.

"Align teams around business goals, not outputs" through outcome-oriented frameworks like OKRs rather than feature checklists.

Based on the search results, I found comprehensive information about RACI matrices for product teams. Here's what I discovered:

## What is RACI?

RACI is an acronym for responsible, accountable, consulted, informed. RACI matrix lays out the responsibility chart for different tasks or deliverables, with the idea to layout the role the product manager and product owner will take against each of these activities.

## Creating a RACI Table

To create a RACI chart, use a spreadsheet or project management software to create a table with columns for tasks or deliverables, responsible parties, accountable parties, consulted parties, and informed parties. Once roles are defined, use a RACI table to organize responsibilities, listing processes as rows and teams as columns, making ownership easy to identify.

## Key Principles

The golden rule of a RACI chart is that every task should have only one accountable owner, with the sole accountable person remaining in charge of approvals and outcomes.

## Application to Product Teams

In the context of product ownership, the RACI matrix serves as a blueprint for defining the roles of product managers, developers, designers, stakeholders, and other team members, ensuring that everyone understands their contributions to the product lifecycle. Tasks or deliverables might include creating a product roadmap, conducting user research, or launching a new feature.

RACI charts define responsibilities for scrum roles, such as product owner and scrum master, and outline participation in events such as sprint planning and code reviews.
